text: 1. The interior design of the newly constructed Parliament building of India incorporates specific national themes for its two houses. Which of the following correctly matches the house with its design theme?

options.text: Lok Sabha: Lotus; Rajya Sabha: Peacock
Lok Sabha: Peacock; Rajya Sabha: Lotus
Lok Sabha: Banyan Tree; Rajya Sabha: Tiger
Lok Sabha: Elephant; Rajya Sabha: Lotus

explanation: In the new Parliament building, the Lok Sabha is themed around the Peacock (India's national bird), and the Rajya Sabha is themed around the Lotus (India's national flower).

text: 2. The delimitation of parliamentary constituencies and the allocation of seats in the Lok Sabha have been frozen until the year 2026. Which two Constitutional Amendments are primarily responsible for this freeze?
explanation: The 42nd Amendment (1976) originally froze the delimitation of constituencies until the year 2000. Later, the 84th Amendment (2001) extended this freeze on the number of seats until 2026 to encourage population control measures.

text: 3. The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003, placed a strict cap on the size of the Council of Ministers (CoM). What is this maximum limit?

options.text: 10% of the total strength of the Rajya Sabha
10% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha
15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha
20% of the total strength of the Parliament

explanation: According to the 91st Amendment Act, the total number of ministers, including the Prime Minister, in the Council of Ministers shall not exceed 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha.

text: 4. In the legislative process of the Indian Parliament, what is the maximum duration the Rajya Sabha can delay an Ordinary Bill before a deadlock is declared and a joint sitting can be summoned?
explanation: For an Ordinary Bill, the Rajya Sabha can delay its passage for a maximum of 6 months. If it is not passed within this period, the President can summon a Joint Sitting of both houses under Article 108. (For Money Bills, the limit is strictly 14 days).

text: 5. According to Article 109 of the Indian Constitution, where must a Money Bill be introduced?

options.text: In a Joint Sitting of both Houses

explanation: Article 109 explicitly states that a Money Bill shall not be introduced in the Council of States (Rajya Sabha). It can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha with the prior recommendation of the President.

text: 6. The practice in the Parliament where all outstanding demands for grants are put to a vote at once, immediately after the expiration of the time allotted for discussion on the Union Budget, is called:
explanation: When the time limit for the discussion of the demands for grants concludes, the Speaker puts all the remaining demands to vote simultaneously, whether they have been discussed or not. This process is officially known as the 'Guillotine'.

text: 7. The Committee on Public Undertakings, one of the crucial financial committees of the Parliament, was created in 1964 on the recommendation of which committee?
explanation: The Committee on Public Undertakings was constituted in 1964 based on the recommendations of the Krishna Menon Committee. It examines the reports and accounts of public sector undertakings (PSUs).

text: 8. Which parliamentary committee is primarily tasked with examining the annual audit reports submitted by the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India?
explanation: The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) scrutinizes the appropriation accounts of the Government of India and the audit reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG). The CAG acts as a 'friend, philosopher, and guide' to the PAC.

text: 9. In the post-independence era, the Estimates Committee was established to examine the budget estimates and suggest economies in public expenditure. In which year was it constituted?
explanation: The Estimates Committee was formed in the year 1950 on the recommendation of John Mathai, the then Finance Minister. It consists of 30 members, all drawn exclusively from the Lok Sabha.

text: 10. The Parliament of India currently utilizes a vast network of Department Related Standing Committees (DRSCs) to ensure deeper scrutiny of legislative and financial proposals. What is the total number of DRSCs currently functioning?
explanation: There are a total of 24 Department Related Standing Committees (DRSCs) in the Indian Parliament. Out of these, 8 work under the Rajya Sabha and 16 under the Lok Sabha. Each committee consists of 31 members (21 from LS and 10 from RS).

text: 11. The Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions classifies and allocates time for bills introduced by private members. Who serves as the ex-officio chairman of this committee in the Lok Sabha?
explanation: The Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha acts as the chairman of the Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions. This committee consists of 15 members in the Lok Sabha.

text: 12. Which constitutional amendment abolished the provision of nominating two members of the Anglo-Indian community to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies?
explanation: The 104th Constitutional Amendment Act (2019) extended the reservation of seats for SCs and STs in the Lok Sabha and states assemblies by ten years but did not extend the provision for the nomination of the Anglo-Indian community, effectively ending it.

text: 13. The Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, commonly known as the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, aims to provide reservations for women in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies. What percentage of seats is reserved under this act?
explanation: The 106th Constitutional Amendment Act provides for a 33% reservation (one-third of total seats) for women in the Lok Sabha, State Legislative Assemblies, and the Legislative Assembly of the NCT of Delhi.

text: 14. Who holds the authority to decide the salaries and allowances of the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha?
explanation: The salaries and allowances of the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker are determined by the Parliament by law and are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.

text: 15. Regarding the dissolution of the lower house of the legislature, which of the following statements is constitutionally correct?

options.text: Only the Prime Minister can advise the dissolution of the Lok Sabha, but a Chief Minister cannot advise the dissolution of the State Assembly.
Both the Prime Minister and the Chief Minister can advise the dissolution of their respective lower houses (Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha) before the expiry of their terms.
The President and Governor can dissolve the respective lower houses at their own discretion without any advice.
The Lok Sabha can be dissolved, but a State Legislative Assembly is a permanent body and cannot be dissolved.

explanation: The Prime Minister can advise the President to dissolve the Lok Sabha, and similarly, the Chief Minister can advise the Governor to dissolve the State Legislative Assembly before their respective 5-year terms expire.

text: 16. Which Article of the Indian Constitution empowers the President to summon a joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament in case of a legislative deadlock over an ordinary bill?
explanation: Article 108 of the Constitution deals with the joint sitting of both Houses in certain cases to resolve a deadlock. The joint sitting is summoned by the President and presided over by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.

text: 17. Who has the final authority to certify whether a particular bill is a 'Money Bill' or not?

options.text: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha

explanation: Under Article 110(3) of the Constitution, if any question arises whether a bill is a Money Bill or not, the decision of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha thereon shall be final.

text: 18. What is the minimum age prescribed by the Constitution to be eligible for membership in the Rajya Sabha (Council of States)?
explanation: According to Article 84, a person must be a citizen of India and not less than 30 years of age to be chosen as a member of the Rajya Sabha. For the Lok Sabha, the minimum age is 25 years.

text: 19. The quorum required to constitute a meeting of either House of Parliament is what fraction of the total number of members of the House?
explanation: The quorum to constitute a meeting of either House of Parliament is one-tenth (1/10th) of the total number of members of that House, including the presiding officer.

text: 20. Which constitutional article provides for the creation or abolition of Legislative Councils (Vidhan Parishad) in the states?
explanation: Article 169 provides for the abolition or creation of Legislative Councils in states. Parliament can create or abolish a Council if the Legislative Assembly of the state passes a resolution to that effect by a special majority.

text: 21. What is the maximum permissible time gap between two sessions of the Parliament?
explanation: According to Article 85, the President shall summon each House of Parliament at such time and place as he thinks fit, but six months shall not intervene between its last sitting in one session and the date appointed for its first sitting in the next session.

text: 22. The term 'Zero Hour' in the context of Indian Parliamentary procedures refers to:

options.text: The time allotted immediately after the Question Hour where members can raise matters of urgent public importance.
The last hour of the parliamentary session before sine die adjournment.
The hour dedicated exclusively to voting on money bills.
The time when the President addresses the joint sitting.

explanation: Zero Hour is an Indian parliamentary innovation (in existence since 1962). It starts immediately after the Question Hour and lasts until the agenda for the day is taken up. During this time, MPs can raise urgent issues without prior notice.

text: 23. In the State Legislature, what is the maximum number of members allowed in the Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha) of a state?
explanation: According to Article 170, the Legislative Assembly of each state shall consist of not more than 500, and not less than 60, members chosen by direct election from territorial constituencies.

text: 24. How many members of the Rajya Sabha are nominated by the President of India for their special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art, or social service?
explanation: Under Article 80, the President nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha who possess special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art, and social service.

text: 25. Which of the following statements about the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) is mathematically correct regarding its composition?

options.text: It consists of 30 members, all from the Lok Sabha.
It consists of 22 members: 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha.
It consists of 22 members: 11 from the Lok Sabha and 11 from the Rajya Sabha.
It consists of 15 members nominated by the President.

explanation: The Public Accounts Committee consists of 22 members—15 elected by the Lok Sabha and 7 elected by the Rajya Sabha. By convention, its chairman is usually from the main opposition party.

text: 26. When a State Legislature passes a bill and sends it to the Governor, the Governor has the power to reserve the bill for the consideration of the President under which Article?
explanation: Under Article 200, when a bill is presented to the Governor after being passed by the state legislature, he may give assent, withhold assent, return the bill, or reserve the bill for the consideration of the President.

text: 27. Who is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha?

options.text: The senior-most member of the Rajya Sabha

explanation: Article 64 states that the Vice-President of India acts as the ex-officio Chairman of the Council of States (Rajya Sabha).

text: 28. What happens to a bill pending in the Lok Sabha when the Lok Sabha is dissolved?

options.text: It is passed on to the newly elected Lok Sabha automatically.
It is transferred to the Rajya Sabha.
The President signs it into an ordinance.

explanation: When the Lok Sabha is dissolved, any bill pending in the Lok Sabha (whether originating in the Lok Sabha or transmitted to it by the Rajya Sabha) lapses. Bills pending in the Rajya Sabha that have not been passed by the Lok Sabha do not lapse.

text: 29. The concept of 'Whip' in the Indian parliamentary system functions to:

options.text: Maintain discipline and ensure attendance and voting by party members according to the party's official stance.
Count the votes during a division in the house.
Adjourn the house due to lack of quorum.

explanation: A 'whip' is an official appointed by a political party to ensure party discipline among its members in the legislature, particularly ensuring that members vote according to the party platform.

text: 30. The 'Prorogation' of a house of Parliament implies:

options.text: Termination of a sitting of the House.
Termination of a session of the House.
Suspension of a Member of Parliament.

explanation: Prorogation means the termination of a session of the House by an order made by the President. Adjournment terminates only a sitting, while dissolution ends the life of the Lok Sabha itself.

text: 31. In the event of a vacancy in the offices of both the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha, who discharges the duties of the Speaker?

options.text: A member of the Lok Sabha appointed by the President
The senior-most member of the Lok Sabha
The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha

explanation: When the offices of both Speaker and Deputy Speaker are vacant, the duties of the office are performed by such member of the Lok Sabha as the President may appoint for the purpose (often referred to as the pro-tem Speaker in other contexts, but here specifically appointed by the President).

text: 32. Under the Anti-Defection Law (Tenth Schedule), who holds the final authority to decide whether a Member of Parliament has incurred disqualification for defection?

options.text: The Presiding Officer of the respective House (Speaker/Chairman)

explanation: According to the Tenth Schedule, the question of disqualification on the ground of defection is decided by the Chairman in the case of Rajya Sabha and the Speaker in the case of Lok Sabha. (However, this decision is subject to judicial review as per the Kihoto Hollohan case).

text: 33. Which article of the Constitution requires an Annual Financial Statement (Budget) to be laid before both Houses of Parliament?
explanation: Article 112 of the Constitution mandates the President to cause to be laid before both Houses of Parliament an 'Annual Financial Statement', commonly known as the Budget, showing estimated receipts and expenditures.

text: 34. Who has the authority to promulgate an Ordinance during the recess of Parliament, functioning as a temporary legislative measure?
explanation: Under Article 123, the President can promulgate an ordinance when either of the two Houses of Parliament is not in session, provided he is satisfied that immediate action is necessary.

text: 35. According to parliamentary procedures, what is a 'Censure Motion'?

options.text: A motion moved to express lack of confidence in the entire Council of Ministers.
A motion moved against an individual minister or a group of ministers for their failure to act or for specific policies.
A motion moved to reduce the amount of demand for a grant.
A motion to draw the attention of the House to a matter of urgent public importance.

explanation: A Censure Motion can be moved against an individual minister, a group of ministers, or the entire council, strictly to censure (strongly criticize) them for specific policies or actions. Unlike a No-Confidence Motion, if passed, the Council of Ministers need not resign.

text: 36. According to Article 100(3) of the Indian Constitution, what is the minimum quorum required to constitute a meeting of either House of Parliament?

options.text: 50 members in Lok Sabha and 25 in Rajya Sabha

explanation: Article 100(3) specifies that the quorum to constitute a meeting of either House of Parliament shall be one-tenth (10%) of the total number of members of the House. If this quorum is not met, Article 100(4) requires the presiding officer to adjourn or suspend the meeting.

text: 37. Under Article 100(1) of the Constitution, when is the Speaker of the Lok Sabha permitted to vote in the House?

options.text: On any ordinary bill but not on Money bills
During the first instance of voting on all resolutions
Only in the case of a tie (casting vote)
During a motion of no-confidence against the government

explanation: Article 100(1) states that the Speaker or Chairman shall not vote in the first instance, but shall have and exercise a 'casting vote' in the case of an equality of votes (a tie).

text: 38. Which Article of the Indian Constitution ensures Parliamentary Immunity by restricting any discussion in Parliament on the conduct of any Supreme Court or High Court judge?
explanation: Article 121 restricts discussion in Parliament with respect to the conduct of any Judge of the Supreme Court or of a High Court in the discharge of his duties, except upon a motion for their removal.

text: 39. To maintain the separation of powers, which Article dictates that courts cannot inquire into the validity of any proceedings of Parliament?
explanation: Article 122 protects the legislature from judicial intervention by stating that the validity of any proceedings in Parliament shall not be called in question on the ground of any alleged irregularity of procedure.

text: 40. The Ordinance Making Power of the President is essentially a temporary legislative power exercised when both Houses of Parliament are not in session. Which Article grants this power?
explanation: Article 123 empowers the President to promulgate ordinances during the recess of Parliament. These ordinances have the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament.

text: 41. What is the maximum theoretical validity period of an ordinance promulgated by the President under Article 123?
explanation: An ordinance must be laid before Parliament within 6 weeks of its reassembly. Since the maximum gap between two parliamentary sessions can be 6 months, the maximum validity of an ordinance without parliamentary approval is 6 months + 6 weeks.

text: 42. Which landmark Supreme Court case is directly related to checking the misuse of the executive's ordinance-making power (frequent re-promulgation without legislative approval)?
explanation: The D.C. Wadhwa Case (1987) is a landmark judgment where the Supreme Court ruled that successive re-promulgation of ordinances without seeking legislative approval is a 'fraud on the Constitution'.

text: 43. All revenues received by the Government of India, including taxes and loans raised, flow into which specific fund controlled by the Parliament?
explanation: Under Article 266, all revenues (taxes, loans, etc.) received by the Government form the Consolidated Fund of India. No money can be withdrawn from it without Parliamentary approval.

text: 44. Government deposits, provident funds, and remittances are stored in which fund, where parliamentary approval is NOT required for disbursements?
explanation: The Public Account of India (also under Article 266) holds public money received by or on behalf of the Government other than those in the Consolidated Fund (like PF deposits, remittances). The executive can make disbursements from it without parliamentary approval, as it operates like a banking transaction.

text: 45. Emergency, unforeseen expenditures by the government are met from which fund under the authority of the President of India?
explanation: The Contingency Fund of India (Article 267) is placed at the disposal of the President to meet unforeseen expenditures pending authorization by Parliament.

text: 46. During the voting on Demands for Grants in Parliament, a member can move a 'Policy Cut' motion to express strong disapproval of the underlying policy. What does this motion propose?

options.text: To reduce the demand amount by ₹100
To reduce the demand amount to exactly ₹1
To reject the entire demand completely
To reduce the demand by a specified lump sum

explanation: A 'Policy Cut' motion states that the amount of the demand be reduced to Re. 1. It signifies sheer disapproval of the policy underlying the demand.

text: 47. Which Article of the Indian Constitution defines and lays down the special provisions regarding 'Financial Bills'?
explanation: Article 117 deals with Financial Bills (Types I and II), which involve matters of revenue and expenditure beyond just the strict definitions of Money Bills (found in Article 110).

text: 48. Under which Article is each House of Parliament empowered to frame its own Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business?
explanation: Article 118 grants each House of Parliament the authority to make rules for regulating its procedure and the conduct of its business.

text: 49. According to Article 120 of the Constitution, the business in Parliament shall be transacted in Hindi or English. However, a member can address the House in their mother tongue under what condition?

options.text: Always, as a matter of fundamental right
With the prior approval of the Prime Minister
With the permission of the Speaker or Chairman
With the permission of the President

explanation: Article 120 states that the Presiding Officer (Speaker in Lok Sabha or Chairman in Rajya Sabha) may permit any member who cannot adequately express himself in Hindi or in English to address the House in his mother tongue.

text: 50. What type of majority is required in the Parliament to pass a law for the creation or abolition of a State Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad)?

options.text: Special Majority + Ratification by half the states
Unanimous vote by the Lok Sabha

explanation: The creation or abolition of a Legislative Council (Article 169), admission/establishment of new states, delimitation, and deciding the salaries of MPs all require only a Simple Majority in Parliament. They are not considered constitutional amendments under Article 368.

text: 51. Which Chapter and range of Articles in Part VI of the Constitution detail the structure and mechanics of the State Legislature?
explanation: Part VI of the Constitution deals with the States. Chapter IV specifically covers the State Legislature from Article 168 to Article 212. (Chapter II deals with the State Executive; Chapter V deals with High Courts).

text: 52. Just as the President has ordinance-making powers at the Union level under Article 123, which Article grants the Governor the power to promulgate ordinances at the State level?
explanation: Article 213 empowers the Governor to promulgate ordinances during the recess of the State Legislature. This mirrors the President's power under Article 123.

text: 53. What is the key difference between a 'Money Bill' and a general 'Financial Bill' regarding their introduction in Parliament?

options.text: A Money Bill can be introduced in either House, while a Financial Bill only in Lok Sabha.
Both must be introduced in the Rajya Sabha first.
A Money Bill can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha with the President's recommendation, whereas certain Financial Bills can be introduced in either House.
A Money Bill requires a Joint Sitting, while a Financial Bill does not.

explanation: Article 109 strictly dictates that Money Bills can ONLY be introduced in the Lok Sabha. Financial Bills of Type II, however, can be introduced in either House. Joint Sittings are explicitly barred for Money Bills.

text: 54. While the President can promulgate an ordinance, he holds the absolute power to withdraw it. When can the President withdraw an ordinance?

options.text: Only within the first 6 weeks of its promulgation
Only after obtaining the Supreme Court's advisory opinion
Anytime at his discretion (on the advice of the Council of Ministers)
Only when the Parliament passes a resolution to that effect

explanation: The President's legislative power to make ordinances includes the power to withdraw them at any time, acting on the advice of the Council of Ministers.

text: 55. If the Parliament decides to increase the salaries and allowances of Members of Parliament, what type of legislative process is required?
explanation: Alteration of salaries and allowances of Members of Parliament falls under procedures that require only a Simple Majority and is not considered a Constitutional Amendment under Article 368.

text: 56. In the Indian legislative system, what is the term used when a sitting of the House is terminated indefinitely without giving a specific date for reconvening?
explanation: Adjournment 'sine die' means terminating a sitting of Parliament for an indefinite period. Prorogation, on the other hand, ends the entire session.

text: 57. Which Constitutional Amendment Act mandated that the total number of Ministers, including the Prime Minister, in the Union Council of Ministers cannot exceed 15% of the Lok Sabha's total strength?
explanation: The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act of 2003 placed a ceiling on the size of the Council of Ministers at both the Central (15% of Lok Sabha) and State levels (15% of State Assembly) to prevent jumbo cabinets.

text: 58. Regarding the delimitation of constituencies, the 84th Constitutional Amendment (2001) froze the total number of Lok Sabha seats. Until which year will this freeze remain in effect?
explanation: The 84th Amendment Act extended the freeze on the total number of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies until the year 2026, building upon the initial freeze implemented by the 42nd Amendment.

text: 59. Which parliamentary committee is popularly associated with being a 'watchdog of public finances' because it examines the CAG reports?
explanation: The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) is tasked with examining the audit reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India, acting as the primary watchdog over the executive's expenditure.

text: 60. Which of the following statements concerning the 'Estimates Committee' of the Indian Parliament is correct?

options.text: It consists of 22 members (15 from Lok Sabha, 7 from Rajya Sabha).
It was established based on the recommendations of the Krishna Menon Committee.
It consists of 30 members, all drawn exclusively from the Lok Sabha.
It is chaired ex-officio by the Finance Minister.

explanation: The Estimates Committee, established in 1950, is unique because its 30 members are exclusively from the Lok Sabha. (PAC has 22 members; Krishna Menon committee recommended the COPU).

text: 61. How many Department Related Standing Committees (DRSCs) currently exist in the Indian Parliament to scrutinize the demands for grants of various ministries?
explanation: There are 24 Department Related Standing Committees (DRSCs), out of which 8 work under the Rajya Sabha and 16 under the Lok Sabha. They play a pivotal role in reviewing bills and budget estimates.

text: 62. The 'Committee on Public Undertakings' (COPU) examines the reports and accounts of public sector units. Under whose recommendation was this committee constituted in 1964?
explanation: The Committee on Public Undertakings was formed in 1964 on the recommendations of the Krishna Menon Committee. Like the PAC, it consists of 22 members.

text: 63. The concept of 'Guillotine' in the Indian Parliamentary process specifically refers to:

options.text: The swift removal of the Prime Minister through a No-Confidence Motion.
Putting all outstanding budget demands for grants to vote simultaneously, even if undiscussed, upon expiry of allotted time.
The President returning a bill for reconsideration.
Expelling a member for unruly behavior.

explanation: When the allotted time for discussion on demands for grants concludes, the Speaker enforces the 'Guillotine', bypassing further debate and putting all remaining demands directly to a vote.

text: 64. The Constitution limits the authority of the Rajya Sabha over a Money Bill. What is the maximum time the Rajya Sabha can withhold a Money Bill before it is deemed passed by both Houses?

options.text: It cannot withhold it at all

explanation: Under Article 109, the Rajya Sabha must return a Money Bill to the Lok Sabha within 14 days, with or without recommendations. If not returned in 14 days, it is deemed to have been passed by both Houses.

text: 65. The Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, granting 33% reservation to women in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies, was enacted through which Constitutional Amendment?
explanation: The 106th Constitutional Amendment Act (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam) provides 33% reservation for women. (Note: The 104th CAA removed Anglo-Indian nominations).

text: 66. During a joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament to resolve a deadlock over an ordinary bill (Article 108), who presides over the session?

options.text: The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Vice President)
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha

explanation: A joint sitting is summoned by the President but is always presided over by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha (or in his absence, the Deputy Speaker). The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha never presides over a joint sitting.

text: 67. In the context of State Legislatures, if a State wants to create a Vidhan Parishad (Legislative Council), it must pass a resolution. What kind of majority is required in the State Legislative Assembly for this resolution?

options.text: Special Majority (2/3rd present & voting + absolute majority of total membership)

explanation: While the Parliament passes the final act with a Simple Majority, the initiating State Legislative Assembly must pass the resolution demanding the creation/abolition of the Council by a Special Majority.

text: 68. Which of the following constitutional provisions applies to both the President (Article 123) and the Governor (Article 213) regarding their ordinance-making power?

options.text: They can issue ordinances even when the legislature is in session.
The ordinances issued are permanent laws immune to judicial review.
Ordinances must be placed before the respective legislature within 6 weeks of its reassembly.
They can only issue ordinances related to the Concurrent List.

explanation: Both Article 123 and Article 213 strictly mandate that any promulgated ordinance must be laid before the Parliament or State Legislature, respectively, and will cease to operate at the expiration of 6 weeks from its reassembly.

text: 69. In the newly constructed Parliament building of India, the interior motifs are heavily inspired by national symbols. The Lok Sabha chamber is designed around which theme?
explanation: The new Parliament building features the Lok Sabha chamber designed with a Peacock theme (National Bird), and the Rajya Sabha chamber designed with a Lotus theme (National Flower).

text: 70. What is the fundamental difference between an Adjournment and Prorogation in parliamentary proceedings?

options.text: Adjournment ends the session, while Prorogation ends the life of the Lok Sabha.
Adjournment suspends a sitting for a specified time, while Prorogation terminates the entire session.
Adjournment is done by the President, while Prorogation is done by the Speaker.
There is no difference; the terms are used interchangeably.

explanation: An Adjournment merely suspends the work in a sitting for a specified time (hours, days). Prorogation, executed by the President, terminates the entire session of the House.

text: 71. Which of the following statements is true regarding the dissolution of the Rajya Sabha?

options.text: It can be dissolved during a severe National Emergency.
It is a continuing house and is immune to dissolution under any circumstance.
It is automatically dissolved every six years.
The President can dissolve it on the advice of the Prime Minister.

explanation: The Rajya Sabha is a continuing house, making it immune to dissolution under any circumstance [1, 2].

text: 72. What is the prescribed term for a member of the Rajya Sabha, and how are their retirements structured?

options.text: 5 years, with half retiring every year.
6 years, with exactly one-third retiring every two years.
6 years, with half retiring every three years.
5 years, with all retiring at the same time.

explanation: Members of the Rajya Sabha serve staggered six-year terms, with exactly one-third of the members retiring every two years [1].

text: 73. In order to create a new All-India Service without disrupting the federal balance, the process must originate via a resolution specifically in which body?
explanation: The creation of a new All-India Service disrupts the federal balance; therefore, the Constitution dictates that this process must originate via a resolution specifically in the Rajya Sabha [3, 4].

text: 74. What is the strict, chronological procedure for the passage of a Money Bill in the Indian Parliament?

options.text: Introduction in Rajya Sabha -> Passage in Lok Sabha -> President's Assent
Introduction in Lok Sabha -> Passage in Lok Sabha -> Transmission to Rajya Sabha -> President's Assent
Introduction in Lok Sabha -> Joint Sitting -> President's Assent
Introduction in either House -> Passage in both -> President's Assent

explanation: The passage of a Money Bill is a strict, linear mechanical process: 1. Introduction in Lok Sabha -> 2. Passage in Lok Sabha -> 3. Transmission to Rajya Sabha (which has limited powers) -> 4. Presentation for President’s assent [1, 4].

text: 75. The Anti-Defection Law, which governs the disqualification of members of Parliament and State Legislatures, was added to the Constitution by which Amendment?
explanation: The Anti-Defection Law was introduced through the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act in 1985, and it is contained in the 10th Schedule of the Constitution [9, 12].

text: 76. Which Constitutional Amendment officially removed the provision for the nomination of Anglo-Indians to the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies?
explanation: The 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2020, led to the removal of the Anglo-Indian nomination from the Lok Sabha and state assemblies [8, 10].

text: 77. The 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023, is a landmark legislation that provides for what specific reservation?

options.text: 33% seats reserved for women in Lok Sabha and State Assemblies
Restoration of SEBC identification power to states

explanation: The 106th Constitutional Amendment Act (CA), 2023, mandates that 1/3rd (33%) of the seats in the Lok Sabha (LS) and Legislative Assemblies (LA) be reserved for women [8, 10].

text: 78. Which of the following parliamentary actions requires only a 'Simple Majority' to be passed?

options.text: Creation or abolition of a Legislative Council
Implementation of the Goods and Services Tax (GST)

explanation: To create or abolish a Legislative Council, as well as for the delimitation of constituencies and deciding MP salaries, only a Simple Majority is required in the Parliament [5].

text: 79. If a State Emergency (President's Rule) is proclaimed, what is the strict parliamentary requirement for its approval?

options.text: Must be approved by Lok Sabha with a special majority within 1 month.
Must be approved by both Houses with a simple majority within 2 months.
Must be approved by both Houses with a special majority within 6 months.
It does not require parliamentary approval.

explanation: A proclamation of President's Rule must be approved by both the Houses of Parliament with a simple majority within 2 months from the date of its issue [13].

text: 80. In the impeachment process of the President of India, what specific role do nominated members of Parliament play?

options.text: They do not participate in either the election or the impeachment.
They participate in the election but not in the impeachment.
They participate in the impeachment, but not in the indirect election.
They have full voting rights in both the election and impeachment.

explanation: Nominated members of Parliament are permitted to participate in the impeachment of the President, but they are explicitly excluded from participating in the President's indirect election via the Electoral College [6, 11].

text: 81. Under Article 100 of the Indian Constitution, if the minimum 10% quorum is not met during a session, what is the duty of the presiding officer?

options.text: To pass bills via emergency ordinance.
To adjourn or suspend the meeting until there is a quorum.
To call for a joint sitting.

explanation: According to Article 100(3), the quorum requires a minimum of 10% of total members [7]. Under Article 100(4), if this quorum is not met, the presiding officer is mandated to adjourn or suspend the meeting [7].

text: 82. The Vice President of India is indirectly elected by an electoral college. This specific electoral college consists of:
explanation: Unlike the President's electoral college, the Vice President is elected by both elected and nominated Members of Parliament (MPs), and state MLAs do not participate [14].

text: 83. To successfully impeach the President of India, what level of majority is constitutionally required in Parliament?

options.text: 2/3rd of members present and voting in both houses
2/3rd of total membership in the first house, and simple majority in the second
2/3rd of total membership in both houses

explanation: The stringent impeachment process requires the first House to pass the resolution by 2/3rd of its total membership, and the second House must also independently approve it by a 2/3rd majority of its total membership [6].

text: 84. If the office of the President becomes vacant due to death, resignation, or removal, who acts as the Acting President?

options.text: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha

explanation: In the event of a vacancy, the Vice President acts as the Acting President [6]. If the Vice President is not available, the Chief Justice of India (CJI) or the senior-most Supreme Court judge takes over [6].

text: 85. Which Constitutional Article provides for the Advocate General of a State, who functions as the state-level equivalent of the Attorney General?
explanation: Article 165 deals with the Advocate General at the state level, who serves as the constitutional equivalent of the Attorney General (Article 76) for the Union level [15, 16].

text: 1. The concept of Fundamental Rights in Part III of the Indian Constitution is primarily inspired by the constitution of which country?
explanation: The Fundamental Rights (Articles 12-35) in the Indian Constitution are inspired by the USA's Bill of Rights. However, the concept of 'Equality before law' under Article 14 is of British origin, while 'Equal protection of laws' is from the USA.

text: 2. The Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) enshrined in Part IV of the Indian Constitution were borrowed from which country?
explanation: DPSPs are borrowed from the Irish Constitution. They serve as guidelines for the central and state governments to ensure social and economic democracy.

text: 3. Which Article of the Indian Constitution explicitly gives the judiciary the power of 'Judicial Review' to declare any law that violates Fundamental Rights as null and void?
explanation: Article 13 establishes the doctrine of judicial review. It states that any law, ordinance, order, or bye-law that infringes upon Fundamental Rights is null and void.

text: 4. Article 15 of the Indian Constitution prohibits discrimination by the State against any citizen on specific grounds. Which of the following is NOT one of the explicitly mentioned grounds?
explanation: Article 15 prohibits discrimination strictly on five grounds: Religion, Race, Caste, Sex, and Place of birth. 'Language' is not explicitly listed as a ground in this article.

text: 5. In the landmark 'Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992)' case, the Supreme Court of India upheld 27% reservation for OBCs but laid down certain conditions. Which of the following was one of those key conditions?

options.text: Reservations must also be applied in promotions.
The 'Creamy layer' among OBCs must be excluded from reservation benefits.
Overall reservation limits can exceed 50% under normal circumstances.
Reservations must be based solely on economic criteria.

explanation: In the Indra Sawhney case, the Supreme Court upheld the 27% OBC reservation but mandated that the 'creamy layer' (advanced sections among OBCs) be excluded, and ruled that there should be no reservation in promotions.

text: 6. Article 19(1) originally guaranteed seven freedoms, but currently guarantees six. Which of the following freedoms is protected under this article?

options.text: Right to strike or declare a bandh
Right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property
Right to form associations or unions

explanation: Article 19(1) guarantees six freedoms (Mnemonic: SAAMRO): Speech, Assemble, Association/Unions, Move freely, Reside/settle, and Occupation. The Right to Property was removed by the 44th Amendment.

text: 7. The expansion of Article 21 to include the 'due process of law' (making it fair, just, and reasonable) rather than just the 'procedure established by law' was a result of which landmark Supreme Court case?
explanation: While the Gopalan case took a narrow view of Article 21, the Menaka Gandhi Case expanded it significantly, ruling that the 'procedure established by law' must be fair, just, and reasonable (essentially introducing the American concept of 'due process').

text: 8. Which Constitutional Amendment Act made the 'Right to Education' a Fundamental Right under Article 21A for children aged 6–14 years?
explanation: The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002, added Article 21A, making free and compulsory education a fundamental right for children between 6 and 14 years. It also shifted the focus of Article 45 in DPSPs to 0-6 years.

text: 9. Under Article 22, a person arrested and detained in custody has certain fundamental protections. Which of the following is NOT one of those immediate protections?

options.text: Right to be informed of the grounds of arrest
Right to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner
Right to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours
Right to an automatic grant of bail within 48 hours

explanation: Article 22 ensures the right to know the reason for arrest, legal counsel, and presentation before a magistrate within 24 hours. It does not grant an automatic right to bail.

text: 10. Article 23 of the Indian Constitution guarantees the Right Against Exploitation. What does this article specifically prohibit?

options.text: Employment of children under 14 in factories
Discrimination on the basis of sex in employment

explanation: Article 23 prohibits human trafficking and forced labor (begar). Article 24 deals with the prohibition of child labor (under 14 years) in hazardous jobs.

text: 11. Under the Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32), the Supreme Court issues various writs. Which writ literally translates to 'We command' and is used to direct a government official to perform their duty?
explanation: Mandamus means 'We command'. It is issued by a court to direct a public official, government, or lower court to perform a mandatory duty they have failed or refused to perform.

text: 12. Which writ is issued to challenge a person's legal right to hold a public office, literally asking 'By what authority?'
explanation: Quo Warranto translates to 'By what authority?'. It is issued to prevent the illegal usurpation of a public office by an individual.

text: 13. While Article 32 empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights, which Article grants concurrent writ jurisdiction to the High Courts?
explanation: Article 226 empowers the High Courts to issue writs. Notably, the High Court's writ jurisdiction is wider than the Supreme Court's, as it can issue writs for Fundamental Rights as well as for 'any other purpose' (ordinary legal rights).

text: 14. During martial law or military rule in any specific area, Fundamental Rights can be suspended. Which Article grants Parliament the power to indemnify actions taken by officials during this period?
explanation: Article 34 provides for the restriction on Fundamental Rights while martial law is in force in any area within the territory of India and empowers Parliament to indemnify government servants for acts done to restore order.

text: 15. The Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSPs) are structurally similar to an administrative feature present in British India. What is that feature?
explanation: DPSPs strongly resemble the 'Instrument of Instructions' issued by the British Government to the Governor-General and Governors of colonies in India under the Government of India Act of 1935.

text: 16. Although DPSPs are not officially classified in the Constitution, scholars categorize them into three types. Which of the following is a 'Gandhian Principle'?

options.text: Article 50: Separation of judiciary and executive

explanation: Article 40 (Village Panchayats) is classified as a Gandhian Principle, along with cottage industries (Art 43), promotion of SC/ST (Art 46), and prohibition of intoxicating drinks (Art 47). Articles 44 and 50 are Liberal-Intellectual, while 39A is Socialist.

text: 17. The famous quote describing DPSPs as a 'cheque drawn on a bank payable at the bank’s own convenience' was stated by:
explanation: K.T. Shah famously criticized the non-justiciable nature of the DPSPs by calling them 'a cheque drawn on a bank payable at the bank’s own convenience.' (Granville Austin called them the 'Conscience of the Constitution').

text: 18. Which of the following Directive Principles of State Policy is classified as a 'Liberal-Intellectual' principle?

options.text: Article 47: Raising the level of nutrition
Article 50: Separation of judiciary and executive

explanation: Article 50 (Separation of judiciary and executive) falls under Liberal-Intellectual principles. Articles 43 and 47 (partially) are Gandhian, and Article 38 is Socialist.

text: 19. The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act (1976) added several new DPSPs to the Constitution. Which of the following was added by this amendment?
explanation: The 42nd Amendment added Articles 39A (Free legal aid), 43A (Workers' participation in management), and 48A (Protection of environment and wildlife).

text: 20. Article 43B, which mandates the state to promote voluntary formation and professional management of Cooperative Societies, was added by which Constitutional Amendment?
explanation: The 97th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2011 gave constitutional status to cooperative societies and added a new DPSP, Article 43B, to promote their autonomous functioning.

text: 21. In the constitutional history of India, which case first established the principle that Fundamental Rights (FRs) prevail over Directive Principles (DPSPs) in case of a conflict?
explanation: The Champakam Dorairajan Case (1951) was the first major judgment where the Supreme Court ruled that in cases of conflict between Fundamental Rights and DPSPs, the Fundamental Rights would prevail.

text: 22. The doctrine that 'a balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is an essential feature of the basic structure of the Constitution' was established in which case?
explanation: In the Minerva Mills Case (1980), the Supreme Court held that the Indian Constitution is founded on the bedrock of the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles, making them both equally important.

text: 23. Which Article under the Right to Freedom of Religion grants linguistic and religious minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice?
explanation: Article 30 grants all minorities (whether based on religion or language) the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice. Article 29 deals with the protection of interests of minorities (conserving language, script, culture).

text: 24. Article 51 of the Directive Principles directs the State to endeavor to:

options.text: Secure a living wage for all workers
Separate the judiciary from the executive

explanation: Article 51 explicitly directs the State to promote international peace and security, maintain just and honorable relations between nations, and foster respect for international law.

text: 25. Which inherent right was recognized as an intrinsic part of the 'Right to Life and Personal Liberty' under Article 21 in the landmark Puttaswamy judgment?
explanation: In the Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) vs Union of India case, a 9-judge Supreme Court bench unanimously ruled that the Right to Privacy is a fundamental right protected under Article 21.

text: 26. Which of the following Fundamental Rights is exclusively available to Indian citizens and NOT to foreigners?

options.text: Article 16: Equal opportunity in public employment
Article 21: Right to life and personal liberty

explanation: Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, and 30 are available exclusively to citizens of India. Therefore, Article 16 (Equal opportunity in public employment) is not available to foreigners.

text: 27. Under Article 12, the definition of 'State' includes which of the following?

options.text: The Government and Parliament of India
The Government and Legislature of each State
Local authorities like Municipalities and Panchayats

explanation: Article 12 broadly defines the 'State' to include the Union and State governments, Parliament, State Legislatures, and all local or other authorities within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India.

text: 28. What is the constitutional validity of Fundamental Duties added by the 42nd Amendment Act?

options.text: They are strictly justiciable and courts can penalize non-compliance directly.
They are non-justiciable, serving as moral/civic obligations for citizens.
They apply to both citizens and non-citizens residing in India.
They override Fundamental Rights in case of conflict.

explanation: Like DPSPs, Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) are non-justiciable in nature. They act as moral and civic obligations for citizens (not foreigners), and the Constitution itself does not provide for direct legal enforcement.

text: 29. Which constitutional article strictly prohibits religious instruction in any educational institution wholly maintained out of State funds?
explanation: Article 28 prohibits the provision of religious instruction in educational institutions wholly maintained out of state funds, upholding the secular character of the state.

text: 30. The Fundamental Right to 'Abolition of Titles' under Article 18 has certain exceptions. Which titles are explicitly permitted by the Constitution?

options.text: Hereditary noble titles like Maharaja or Nawab
Titles conferred by foreign states to Indian citizens
Titles based on wealth and land ownership

explanation: Article 18 prohibits the State from conferring any titles except those that are military (e.g., General, Major) or academic (e.g., Doctor, Professor) distinctions.

text: 31. What is the fundamental difference in the amendment process between an Ordinary Right and a Fundamental Right?

options.text: An ordinary right cannot be amended, while a fundamental right can.
An ordinary right requires a constitutional amendment, while a fundamental right requires a simple majority.
An ordinary right is amended by a simple majority via ordinary law, while a fundamental right requires a Constitutional Amendment.
There is no difference; both require identical legislative procedures.

explanation: Ordinary rights are protected by ordinary laws and can be changed by the legislature with a simple majority. Fundamental rights are protected by the Constitution and can only be altered through a formal Constitutional Amendment (Special Majority).

text: 32. Under the Directive Principles of State Policy, what does Article 39A explicitly direct the State to provide?

options.text: Equal justice and free legal aid

explanation: Added by the 42nd Amendment Act (1976), Article 39A directs the State to promote equal justice and to provide free legal aid to the poor, ensuring that justice is not denied due to economic disabilities.

text: 33. Which article grants Parliament the absolute power to restrict or abrogate the Fundamental Rights of the members of the armed forces to ensure discipline?
explanation: Article 33 empowers Parliament to restrict or abrogate the fundamental rights of members of the armed forces, paramilitary forces, police forces, and intelligence agencies to ensure the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline.

text: 34. The Supreme Court established that Parliament has the power to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, provided it does not alter its 'Basic Structure'. Which case established this doctrine?
explanation: The landmark Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973) established the 'Basic Structure Doctrine', ruling that while Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights (overruling the Golak Nath case), it cannot destroy or alter the basic structure of the Constitution.

text: 35. According to Article 37 of the Constitution, what is the exact legal status of the Directive Principles of State Policy?

options.text: They are directly enforceable by the Supreme Court.
They are legally binding on state governments but not the central government.
They are non-justiciable in any court but are fundamental in the governance of the country.
They can be invoked only during a National Emergency.

explanation: Article 37 declares that the DPSPs are not enforceable by any court (non-justiciable), but they are nonetheless 'fundamental in the governance of the country' and it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws.

text: 36. The inclusion of Fundamental Duties in Part IV-A of the Indian Constitution was originally recommended by which committee?
explanation: The Sardar Swaran Singh Committee (1976) was constituted during the National Emergency to make recommendations about fundamental duties, leading to the 42nd Amendment Act.

text: 37. The Swaran Singh Committee recommended the inclusion of 8 Fundamental Duties, but the 42nd Amendment Act added 10. Which of the following was a recommendation by the committee that was REJECTED and not included in the Constitution?

options.text: Duty to respect the National Flag and Anthem
Duty of citizens to pay taxes

explanation: The Swaran Singh Committee suggested incorporating a duty to pay taxes and provisions for punishing non-compliance with duties. Both of these recommendations were rejected by the government and not included in Article 51A.

text: 38. The 11th Fundamental Duty, which mandates parents or guardians to provide opportunities for education to their children between 6 and 14 years, was added by which Constitutional Amendment?
explanation: The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2002 made primary education a fundamental right (Art 21A), changed the scope of DPSP Article 45, and added the 11th Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(k).

text: 39. Unlike certain Fundamental Rights (such as Articles 14 and 21) which are available to foreigners, Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) apply to:

options.text: Both citizens and non-citizens residing in India
Only public servants and government officials

explanation: Fundamental Duties are strictly confined to Indian citizens only and do not extend to foreigners residing in India.

text: 40. Which committee evaluated the existence of legal provisions for the implementation of some of the Fundamental Duties (e.g., mapping the Wildlife Protection Act to the duty of protecting the environment)?
explanation: The Justice Verma Committee (1999) identified the existence of legal provisions (like the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, IPC sections, and Wildlife Act) that enforce specific Fundamental Duties.

text: 41. Article 14 guarantees 'Equality before the law', but it is not absolute. Who among the following enjoys constitutional immunity from criminal proceedings during their term of office?

options.text: President of India and State Governors

explanation: As an exception to Article 14, the President of India and State Governors enjoy immunity from civil (partially) and criminal proceedings during their term of office.

text: 42. Article 19(1) guarantees the freedom of speech and expression. However, under Article 19(2), the State can impose reasonable restrictions. Which of the following is a valid ground for such restriction?

options.text: Sovereignty, security, decency, and public order
Criticism of the ruling government's manifesto

explanation: Article 19(2) provides that the right to freedom of speech can be reasonably restricted on grounds like sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the state, friendly relations with foreign states, public order, decency, or morality.

text: 43. Which prerogative writ literally means 'Produce the body' and is issued by a court to protect an individual against arbitrary and unlawful detention?
explanation: Habeas Corpus means 'to have the body of'. It is a bulwark of individual liberty against arbitrary detention, commanding the detainer to bring the detainee before the court.

text: 44. What is the fundamental difference between the writs of 'Prohibition' and 'Certiorari'?

options.text: Prohibition is issued against public authorities, while Certiorari is issued against private individuals.
Prohibition is issued to stop a lower court before it makes a final order, while Certiorari is issued to squash an order after it has been made.
Prohibition is issued only by the Supreme Court, while Certiorari is issued only by High Courts.
Prohibition challenges a person's legal right to hold office, while Certiorari transfers cases.

explanation: Prohibition is preventive (stopping a lower court from exceeding jurisdiction during pending proceedings), whereas Certiorari is curative (transferring a case or squashing an order that has already been passed by the lower court).

text: 45. Article 20 of the Indian Constitution provides protection against arbitrary conviction. Which of the following doctrines is NOT a component of Article 20?

options.text: No ex post facto law (Retrospective criminal legislation)
No double jeopardy (Punished twice for the same offense)
No self-incrimination (Forced to be a witness against oneself)
Protection against preventive detention beyond 3 months

explanation: Protection against preventive detention beyond 3 months (without an advisory board's approval) is a provision under Article 22, not Article 20. Article 20 deals with ex post facto laws, double jeopardy, and self-incrimination.

text: 46. In which landmark case did the Supreme Court establish that the 'Right to travel abroad' is an integral part of 'personal liberty' guaranteed under Article 21?
explanation: The Satwant Singh Case (and later deeply reinforced in the Menaka Gandhi case) affirmed that the Right to travel abroad falls under the ambit of 'personal liberty' within Article 21.

text: 47. Which Article of the Indian Constitution explicitly prohibits the employment of children below the age of 14 years in hazardous jobs like factories and mines?
explanation: Article 24 strictly prohibits the employment of children under 14 years of age in hazardous occupations. (Article 23 prohibits human trafficking and forced labor/begar).

text: 48. While Fundamental Rights can generally be suspended during a National Emergency (Article 352), which two articles cannot be suspended under any circumstances?
explanation: The 44th Amendment Act of 1978 mandated that the Fundamental Rights guaranteed by Articles 20 (protection in respect of conviction) and 21 (right to life and personal liberty) remain active even during a National Emergency.

text: 49. Article 26 of the Constitution grants the right to manage religious affairs. However, similar to Article 25, this right is subject to specific restrictions. What are they?
explanation: Articles 25 and 26 (Freedom of Religion) are explicitly subject to public order, morality, and health, meaning the state can intervene if religious practices threaten these domains.

text: 50. Which Fundamental Right ensures that a citizen cannot be compelled to pay any taxes specifically meant for the promotion or maintenance of any particular religion?
explanation: Article 27 ensures the secular nature of the state by prohibiting it from spending public tax money on the promotion or maintenance of any specific religion.

text: 51. Regarding Articles 29 and 30 (Cultural and Educational Rights), how does the Indian Constitution define the term 'Minority'?

options.text: Any community comprising less than 10% of the state's population.
Any non-Hindu community residing in India.
The Constitution identifies them purely on economic grounds.
The Constitution does not define the term 'minority' anywhere.

explanation: The term 'minority' is not defined anywhere in the Constitution. However, it identifies minorities on two grounds for constitutional protection: religious and linguistic (recognized dynamically by the Supreme Court/Government).

text: 52. When analyzing the writ jurisdiction of courts in India, which of the following statements is constitutionally accurate?

options.text: The Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction under Article 32 is wider than the High Court's under Article 226.
The High Court's writ jurisdiction under Article 226 is wider because it can issue writs for both Fundamental Rights and ordinary legal rights.
Only the Supreme Court can issue the writ of Quo Warranto.
High Courts can only issue writs during a National Emergency.

explanation: Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights AND 'for any other purpose' (ordinary legal rights). Article 32 restricts the Supreme Court strictly to the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.

text: 53. Following the Golak Nath case (1967) which ruled that Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights, the Parliament passed an amendment asserting its power to amend any part of the Constitution. Which amendment was this?
explanation: The 24th Amendment Act (1971) was enacted specifically to overcome the Golak Nath verdict, declaring that Parliament has the power to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, under Article 368.

text: 54. The 25th Constitutional Amendment (1971) inserted a unique clause regarding the relationship between FRs and DPSPs. It stated that laws enacted to give effect to which specific Directive Principles cannot be struck down for violating Articles 14 and 19?
explanation: The 25th Amendment secured primacy for Article 39(b) [equitable distribution of material resources] and 39(c) [prevention of concentration of wealth] over the Fundamental Rights guaranteed by Articles 14 and 19.

text: 55. Which Article of the Directive Principles of State Policy directs the State to secure the 'Right to work, to education and to public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement'?
explanation: Article 41 falls under Socialist Principles, directing the state to provide the right to work, education, and public assistance to marginalized demographics subject to its economic capacity.

text: 56. Providing 'just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief' is a goal outlined in which Directive Principle of State Policy?
explanation: Article 42 is a socialist DPSP that requires the state to make provisions for securing just and humane conditions of work and for maternity relief.

text: 57. According to the ideological classification of Directive Principles, Article 46 deals with the promotion of educational and economic interests of SCs, STs, and other weaker sections. This is classified as a:
explanation: Article 46 is classified as a Gandhian Principle, reflecting Gandhi's vision for the upliftment of marginalized sections of society (Harijans/Dalits) and protecting them from social injustice.

text: 58. Which Constitutional Amendment updated Article 38 of the DPSP, adding a clause that specifically directs the State to 'minimize the inequalities in income, status, facilities, and opportunities'?
explanation: While the 42nd Amendment added many DPSPs (39A, 43A, 48A), the 44th Amendment Act (1978) updated Article 38 to further minimize inequalities, acting as a counter-balance post-Emergency.

text: 59. Article 51A outlines the Fundamental Duties of Indian citizens. Which specific clause corresponds to the duty 'to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood amongst all the people of India... and to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women'?
explanation: Article 51A(e) explicitly commands citizens to promote harmony across religious/linguistic diversities and to renounce practices that are derogatory to the dignity of women.

text: 60. The duty to 'develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform' is found under which clause of the Fundamental Duties?
explanation: Article 51A(h) is a hallmark progressive duty asking citizens to develop a scientific temper, humanism, and the spirit of inquiry to combat superstition and orthodox regression.

text: 61. The 42nd Amendment Act added Article 48A to the Directive Principles. What does Article 48A specifically mandate the State to do?

options.text: Organize agriculture and animal husbandry on modern lines.
Prohibit the slaughter of cows and calves.
Protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife.

explanation: While Article 48 (a Gandhian/Liberal principle) deals with agriculture, animal husbandry, and prohibiting cow slaughter, Article 48A strictly deals with Environmental protection.

text: 62. Which of the following constitutional provisions directs the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State?
explanation: Article 50 is a Liberal-Intellectual Directive Principle that mandates the separation of the judiciary from the executive to ensure independent judicial functioning.

text: 63. The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act (1992), which institutionalized the Panchayati Raj system across India, gave practical shape to which Directive Principle?
explanation: Article 40 (a Gandhian Principle) directs the state to organize village panchayats and endow them with necessary powers. The 73rd Amendment realized this goal structurally.

text: 64. The Kaka Kalelkar Commission (1953) is historically significant in relation to Article 15 and 16 because it was the first commission established to:

options.text: Investigate the implementation of the Uniform Civil Code.
Identify and recommend measures for Socially and Educationally Backward Classes (OBCs).
Redraw state boundaries on linguistic lines.
Draft the framework for Fundamental Duties.

explanation: The Kaka Kalelkar Commission was the First Backward Classes Commission setup to identify socially and educationally backward classes. (The Mandal Commission was the second).

text: 65. The term 'Procedure established by law' under Article 21 was initially interpreted narrowly in the Gopalan Case. What was the exact limitation of this narrow interpretation?

options.text: It protected individuals against arbitrary executive action, but not against arbitrary legislative action.
It protected individuals only in civil cases, not criminal.
It was only applicable to Indian citizens, excluding foreigners.
It allowed courts to invalidate laws if they felt the laws were 'unreasonable'.

explanation: In the Gopalan Case (1950), the SC ruled that Article 21 only provides protection against arbitrary executive action. If a legislature passes an arbitrary law depriving someone of their life/liberty, the court couldn't strike it down. The Menaka Gandhi case (1978) reversed this by introducing the 'due process' concept (laws must be fair, just, and reasonable).

text: 66. Article 18 deals with the Abolition of Titles. Under this article, what is the protocol for an Indian citizen accepting a title from a foreign State?

options.text: They can accept it with the prior approval of the Prime Minister.
They can accept it freely as long as it is not a military title.
They can accept it with the prior consent of the President.
An Indian citizen is absolutely prohibited from accepting any title from any foreign State.

explanation: Article 18(2) strictly prohibits any citizen of India from accepting any title from any foreign State. (Only foreigners holding an office of profit under the State need the President's consent to accept a title).

text: 67. A person seeking enforcement of their Fundamental Rights moves the Supreme Court under Article 32. However, for a violation of an 'Ordinary Legal Right', what constitutional remedy is available?

options.text: The person can still use Article 32.
There is no constitutional remedy for ordinary legal rights.
The person must move the High Court using its wider writ jurisdiction under Article 226.
The person must directly petition the President of India.

explanation: While Article 32 is strictly for Fundamental Rights violations, Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs for both Fundamental Rights and any other ordinary legal rights.

text: 68. Which specific Directive Principle corresponds to the goal of the 'Protection of monuments and places and objects of national importance'?
explanation: Article 49 is a Liberal-Intellectual principle that obligates the State to protect every monument or place of artistic or historic interest declared to be of national importance from spoliation and destruction.

text: 69. What was the central ruling of the Supreme Court in the landmark 'Minerva Mills Case' (1980) regarding the relationship between Fundamental Rights and DPSPs?

options.text: Fundamental Rights are absolutely supreme and DPSPs have no legal standing.
DPSPs always override Fundamental Rights in matters of economic policy.
The Indian Constitution is founded on the bedrock of the balance between Fundamental Rights and DPSPs, making them equally essential.
Parliament is prohibited from amending either FRs or DPSPs.

explanation: In the Minerva Mills case, the Supreme Court struck down a provision of the 42nd Amendment that gave total primacy to DPSPs over FRs. The Court ruled that harmony and balance between the two is an essential feature of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.

text: 70. Article 23 prohibits traffic in human beings and 'begar'. What does the term 'begar' mean in historical and constitutional context?

options.text: Denial of equal wages to women

explanation: Begar is a system of forced labor under which people are compelled to work without receiving any remuneration, a practice strictly prohibited under Article 23.

text: 71. Article 22 provides protection against arrest and preventive detention. What is the maximum duration a person can be kept under preventive detention without the approval of an advisory board?
explanation: According to Article 22, protection from preventive detention extends such that a person cannot be detained for more than 3 months unless an advisory board (consisting of high court judges) reports sufficient cause for extended detention.

text: 72. Which Article explicitly states that the power to make laws for giving effect to certain specified Fundamental Rights (like prescribing punishments under Art 17 and 23, or restrictions under Art 33) vests ONLY with the Parliament and not state legislatures?
explanation: Article 35 lays down that the power to make laws to give effect to certain specified fundamental rights shall vest only in the Parliament and not in the state legislatures, ensuring uniformity of fundamental rights across India.

text: 73. The Mandal Commission (1979), which recommended 27% reservation for OBCs (later upheld in the Indra Sawhney case), was officially implemented by the government led by which Prime Minister?
explanation: While the Mandal Commission (Second Backward Classes Commission) was set up in 1979, its recommendations for a 27% reservation for OBCs in public employment were implemented later by the V.P. Singh government.

text: 74. The Indian Constitution balances Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles. Which prominent constitutional expert described the Directive Principles as the 'Conscience of the Constitution'?
explanation: Granville Austin famously described the Directive Principles of State Policy (along with Fundamental Rights) as the 'Conscience of the Constitution'.

text: 75. Who among the following scholars or leaders referred to the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) as a 'Manifesto of Aims & Aspirations'?
explanation: K.C. Wheare described the DPSPs as a 'Manifesto of Aims & Aspirations'. (Note: K.T. Shah called it a 'cheque payable at the bank's convenience', and B.N. Rau called them 'Moral Precepts').

text: 76. When analyzing the fundamental differences between Fundamental Rights (FRs) and Directive Principles (DPSPs), which of the following statements is conceptually correct?

options.text: FRs are positive obligations of the state, while DPSPs are negative obligations.
FRs aim to promote social democracy, while DPSPs promote political democracy.
FRs are negative obligations that restrict the state, while DPSPs are positive obligations directing the state to act.
Both FRs and DPSPs are legally justiciable in the Supreme Court.

explanation: Fundamental Rights are generally negative obligations (they prohibit the State from doing certain things to protect political democracy). DPSPs are positive obligations (they require the State to take action to promote social and economic democracy).

text: 77. Which specific clause of the Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) mandates citizens to 'abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem'?
explanation: Article 51A(a) is the very first fundamental duty, which requires Indian citizens to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals, the National Flag, and the National Anthem.

text: 78. Article 51A(b) outlines a Fundamental Duty related to the history of India. What does it ask citizens to do?

options.text: To value and preserve the composite culture
To defend the country and render national service
To cherish and follow the noble ideals of the freedom struggle

explanation: Article 51A(b) directs citizens to cherish and follow the noble ideals that inspired our national struggle for freedom.

text: 79. The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act [UAPA] of 1967 is a legal statute that provides practical backing to which specific Fundamental Duty?

options.text: Article 51A (c): Upholding and protecting the sovereignty, unity, and integrity of India

explanation: The Justice Verma Committee identified that the UAPA (1967) provides a strong legal framework to enforce the Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(c), which is to uphold and protect India's sovereignty, unity, and integrity.

text: 80. Which Fundamental Duty specifically instructs citizens to 'value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture'?
explanation: Article 51A(f) mandates every citizen to value and preserve the rich heritage of the country's composite culture.

text: 81. The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act (1971) was enacted to ensure compliance with which constitutional provision?

options.text: Article 51A (a): Respect for the National Flag and Anthem

explanation: The National Honour Act (1971) prevents the desecration of or insult to the National Flag, National Anthem, and the Constitution, directly enforcing the Fundamental Duty specified in Article 51A(a).

text: 82. The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act (2002) significantly altered the educational framework in the Constitution. Besides adding Article 21A and Article 51A(k), how did it change Article 45?

options.text: It mandated free higher education for all women.
It shifted its focus to require the State to provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete the age of 6 years.
It removed Article 45 from the Directive Principles entirely.
It made agricultural education compulsory in rural areas.

explanation: Originally, Article 45 asked the state to provide free education for children up to 14 years. After the 86th Amendment made 6-14 years a Fundamental Right (Art 21A), the text of Article 45 was amended to focus on early childhood care and education for children aged 0-6 years.

text: 83. Which Socialist Directive Principle, added by the 42nd Amendment Act (1976), requires the State to take steps to secure the 'participation of workers in the management of industries'?
explanation: Article 43A was added by the 42nd CAA (1976) to ensure workers' participation in the management of industries. (Article 43 is about a living wage, and 43B is about Cooperative Societies).

text: 84. The Directive Principle under Article 47 serves a dual purpose. It directs the State to raise the level of nutrition and the standard of living, and also includes a Gandhian principle to prohibit:

options.text: The slaughter of cows and calves
Intoxicating drinks and drugs that are injurious to health

explanation: Article 47 mandates the State to improve public health and nutrition, specifically highlighting the prohibition of the consumption of intoxicating drinks and drugs (a core Gandhian ideal).

text: 85. Article 48 of the Directive Principles instructs the State to organize agriculture and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines. What specific prohibition is included in this article?

options.text: Prohibition of the slaughter of cows, calves, and other milch and draught cattle

explanation: Article 48 incorporates the Gandhian principle of preserving cattle wealth, explicitly directing the State to prohibit the slaughter of cows, calves, and other milch/draught cattle.

text: 86. Under the Fundamental Duties, which clause instructs citizens 'to safeguard public property and to abjure violence'?
explanation: Article 51A(i) explicitly directs all citizens to safeguard public property and to abjure (renounce) violence.

text: 87. Which Fundamental Duty encourages Indian citizens to 'strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity' so that the nation constantly rises?
explanation: Article 51A(j) is the progressive duty that calls upon individuals to strive for excellence in all personal and collective spheres to ensure the nation's continuous growth.

text: 88. In the event of an unlawful or arbitrary detention, the courts can issue the writ of 'Habeas Corpus'. To whom is this writ primarily addressed?

options.text: To the legislative assembly of the state
To the lower court judge who ordered the detention
To the detaining authority (police or individual) commanding them to produce the detainee

explanation: Habeas Corpus ('produce the body') is addressed to the person or authority who has detained another unlawfully, commanding them to bring the detained person physically before the court.

text: 89. B.N. Rau, the Constitutional Advisor to the Constituent Assembly, described the Directive Principles of State Policy using which phrase?

options.text: Heart and Soul of the Constitution

explanation: B.N. Rau described the DPSPs as 'Moral Precepts' for the authorities of the state. (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'Heart and Soul').
