text: 12. What is the specific nomination requirement for a candidate contesting the Vice Presidential election?
explanation: To contest the Vice Presidential election, a candidate requires at least 20 electors as proposers and 20 electors as seconders. For the President, it is 50 proposers and 50 seconders [3].

text: 13. In case of an election dispute related to the President or the Vice President, which authority holds the final power to decide?
explanation: Under Article 71, all doubts and disputes arising out of or in connection with the election of a President or Vice President are inquired into and decided exclusively by the Supreme Court [3].

text: 14. A candidate contesting for the post of the President of India is required to make a security deposit of what amount in the Reserve Bank of India?
explanation: A candidate for the Presidential election must make a security deposit of ₹15,000 in the Reserve Bank of India, which is forfeited if they fail to secure 1/6th of the valid votes polled [4].

text: 15. What is the fundamental qualification requirement for a person to contest for the office of the Vice President regarding legislative membership?

options.text: Must be qualified for election as a member of the Lok Sabha
Must be qualified for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha
Must already be a sitting MP
Must be qualified to be a Supreme Court Judge

explanation: A candidate for Vice President must be qualified for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha. Conversely, a candidate for President must be qualified for election as a member of the Lok Sabha [3].

text: 16. The Vice President is the ex-officio:
explanation: According to Article 64, the Vice President of India serves as the ex-officio Chairman of the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) and shall not hold any other office of profit [3].

text: 17. Which unique Vice President acted as the President of India on three separate occasions?
explanation: Mohammad Hidayatullah holds the unique distinction of having acted as President of India three times. He was the Chief Justice of India and later became the Vice President [3].

text: 18. Article 61 provides the procedure for the Impeachment of the President. What is the only constitutional ground upon which the President can be impeached?
explanation: Under Article 61, the President can be impeached from office for the 'Violation of the Constitution'. The Constitution, however, does not define the meaning of this phrase.

text: 19. In the context of the President's impeachment process, which of the following groups participates in the impeachment but does NOT participate in their election?

options.text: Nominated members of either House of Parliament
Elected members of State Legislative Assemblies
Members of the State Legislative Councils

explanation: Nominated members of Parliament do not vote in the election of the President. However, they are legally permitted to vote and participate in the impeachment process of the President.

text: 20. Which of the following groups votes in the election of the President but does NOT participate in their impeachment?

options.text: Elected members of State Legislative Assemblies (MLAs)
Elected members of the Rajya Sabha

explanation: Elected MLAs form a core part of the Electoral College that elects the President. However, the impeachment process is purely a parliamentary function, and MLAs have no role in it.

text: 21. Under Article 72, the President has the power to grant pardons. How does this power fundamentally differ from the Governor's pardoning power under Article 161?

options.text: Only the Governor can pardon a death sentence.
The Governor's pardon cannot apply to state laws.
Only the President can grant a pardon in cases involving a death sentence or a court-martial.
Both hold identical powers with no difference.

explanation: While both possess pardoning powers, only the President has the exclusive power to pardon sentences inflicted by a Court Martial (military court) and sentences of death.

text: 22. The President of India can promulgate an ordinance under Article 123 only when:

options.text: A National Emergency is in active effect
At least one House of Parliament is not in session
The Supreme Court advises him to do so

explanation: Article 123 empowers the President to issue ordinances when Parliament is in recess (i.e., when either both Houses or at least one House is not in session), as a law requires both Houses to pass it.

text: 23. Which President of India historically exercised the 'Pocket Veto' in 1986 over the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill?
explanation: President Giani Zail Singh famously used the Pocket Veto (taking no action on a bill for an indefinite period) against the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill in 1986, which threatened freedom of the press.

text: 24. The President of India possesses the 'Suspensive Veto' power, which means they can return a bill to Parliament for reconsideration. However, this veto CANNOT be used against which type of bill?
explanation: The President cannot return a Money Bill for reconsideration. They must either give or withhold their assent, primarily because a Money Bill is introduced with their prior recommendation.

text: 25. By virtue of the 24th Constitutional Amendment Act (1971), the President has NO veto power whatsoever in respect to:

options.text: Ordinary Bills passed during an Emergency

explanation: The 24th Amendment made it constitutionally obligatory for the President to give their assent to Constitutional Amendment Bills, stripping them of any veto power over such bills.

text: 26. When the office of the President falls vacant due to resignation, removal, death, or otherwise, the Vice-President acts as President. What is the maximum period they can act in this capacity?
explanation: Under Article 62, an election to fill a vacancy in the office of the President must be held within 6 months. Hence, the Vice President can act as President for a maximum of 6 months.

text: 27. Who among the following has the constitutional authority to summon a joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament in case of a legislative deadlock?
explanation: Under Article 108, it is the President who has the legislative power to summon a joint sitting of both Houses. However, the sitting is presided over by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.

text: 28. Who administers the oath of office to the President of India as mandated by Article 60?
explanation: The oath of the President is administered by the Chief Justice of India, and in their absence, by the senior-most judge of the Supreme Court available.

text: 29. If the President wishes to resign from their office before the expiration of their 5-year term, to whom must they address their resignation letter?
explanation: According to Article 56(1)(a), the President can resign from office by writing under their hand addressed to the Vice-President.

text: 30. To whom does the Vice President of India submit their letter of resignation?
explanation: The Vice President may resign from their office at any time by submitting a resignation letter addressed to the President of India.

text: 31. The 70th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1992 altered the Electoral College for the President. Which new members were added to participate in the election?

options.text: Nominated members of the Rajya Sabha
Elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry

explanation: The 70th Amendment Act expanded the Electoral College for the President to explicitly include the elected members of the legislative assemblies of the National Capital Territory of Delhi and the Union Territory of Puducherry.

text: 32. Under the discretionary powers of the President, in which specific scenario can they exercise personal discretion in appointing the Prime Minister?

options.text: When a single party gets an absolute majority
When no single party or coalition secures a clear majority in the Lok Sabha
When a Money Bill is defeated in Parliament
When the President disagrees with the current cabinet's policies

explanation: The President has situational discretion to appoint the Prime Minister when no political party secures a clear majority (a hung parliament) or when the incumbent PM dies suddenly without an obvious successor.

text: 33. Which of the following Presidents holds the distinction of being the first to die while in office?
explanation: Dr. Zakir Husain (1967-1969) was the first President of India to die while in office. Following his death, V. V. Giri became the acting President.

text: 34. Regarding the Vice President acting as the President (Article 65), which of the following statements is constitutionally accurate?

options.text: The Vice President continues to draw the salary of the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
The Vice President continues to perform the duties of the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
The Vice President is entitled to the salary and privileges of the President.
The Vice President requires parliamentary approval to act as President.

explanation: When acting as President, the Vice President ceases to perform the duties of the Chairman of Rajya Sabha and draws the salary, allowances, and privileges of the President.

text: 35. If the offices of both the President and the Vice-President fall vacant simultaneously, who acts as the President of India?
explanation: According to the President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969, if both offices are vacant, the Chief Justice of India (or in their absence, the senior-most judge of the SC) acts as the President. This occurred in 1969 with CJI M. Hidayatullah.

text: 36. Under Article 72, the President has various pardoning powers. Which term describes the substitution of one form of punishment for a lighter form (e.g., a death sentence substituted with rigorous imprisonment)?
explanation: Commutation denotes the substitution of one form of punishment for a lighter form. For example, a death sentence may be commuted to rigorous imprisonment.

text: 37. Which pardoning power involves reducing the period of a sentence without changing its character (e.g., reducing rigorous imprisonment from two years to one year)?
explanation: Remission implies reducing the period of the sentence without changing its essential character. The punishment remains the same type but for a shorter duration.

text: 38. What does the President's pardoning power of 'Respite' specifically entail?

options.text: Completely absolving the convict from all sentences and disqualifications.
A temporary stay of the execution of a sentence, especially a death sentence.
Awarding a lesser sentence in place of one originally awarded due to a special fact, such as physical disability or pregnancy.
Reducing the duration of the sentence without altering its nature.

explanation: Respite denotes awarding a lesser sentence in place of the originally awarded one due to a special fact, such as the physical disability of a convict or the pregnancy of a female offender.

text: 39. The President can grant a 'Reprieve' to a convict. What is the primary purpose of a reprieve?

options.text: To change a death sentence to life imprisonment.
To stay the execution of a sentence (especially death) for a temporary period to enable the convict to seek a pardon or commutation.
To reduce the fine imposed by a court.
To completely erase the criminal record of the convict.

explanation: Reprieve implies a stay of the execution of a sentence (especially that of death) for a temporary period. Its purpose is to enable the convict to have time to seek pardon or commutation from the President.

text: 40. In the history of Indian Presidential elections, who holds the unique distinction of being elected unopposed?
explanation: Neelam Sanjiva Reddy is the only President of India to have been elected unopposed (in 1977), after a previous unsuccessful bid for the presidency.

text: 41. During which President's election did the returning officers have to count the 'second preference' votes to declare a winner, the only such instance in Indian history?
explanation: In the 1969 Presidential election, V.V. Giri won the election after the counting of the second preference votes, as no candidate secured the required quota in the first count.

text: 42. The Constitution of India explicitly provides 'Constitutional Discretion' to which of the following executive heads?

options.text: Both the President and the Governor
Neither the President nor the Governor

explanation: While both the President and Governor have 'Situational Discretion' (e.g., appointing a PM/CM in a hung assembly), the Constitution explicitly grants 'Constitutional Discretion' ONLY to the Governor under Article 163. The President has no constitutional discretion.

text: 43. Under Article 80 of the Constitution, the President has the power to nominate 12 members to the Rajya Sabha. From which of the following fields are these members NOT nominated?
explanation: Under Article 80, the President nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha who have special knowledge or practical experience in: Literature, Science, Art, and Social Service (Trick: LSAS). 'Sports' is not explicitly mentioned, though sportspersons are sometimes nominated under 'Art' or 'Social Service'.

text: 44. The President of India causes various constitutional reports to be laid before the Parliament. Which of the following reports is NOT laid by the President?

options.text: Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG)
Report of the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC)
Report of the Public Accounts Committee (PAC)

explanation: The President lays the reports of constitutional bodies like the CAG, UPSC, Finance Commission, NCSC, and NCST before Parliament. The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) is a parliamentary committee that submits its own report directly to the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.

text: 45. To introduce a 'Money Bill' in the Lok Sabha under Article 110, whose prior recommendation is constitutionally mandatory?

options.text: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha

explanation: A Money Bill can be introduced in the Lok Sabha only on the prior recommendation of the President. (Note: The Speaker decides *whether* a bill is a Money Bill, but the President *recommends* its introduction).

text: 46. Article 267 establishes the Contingency Fund of India. At whose disposal is this fund placed to meet unforeseen expenditures pending parliamentary approval?
explanation: The Contingency Fund of India is placed at the disposal of the President of India. He can make advances out of it to meet unforeseen expenditure pending its authorization by Parliament.

text: 47. According to Article 77 of the Indian Constitution, all executive actions of the Government of India shall be expressed to be taken in the name of the:
explanation: Article 77 states that all executive action of the Government of India shall be expressed to be taken in the name of the President, and he makes rules for the more convenient transaction of government business.

text: 48. Under Article 76, the President appoints the highest law officer in the country who gives advice to the Government of India upon legal matters. Name this office.
explanation: The President appoints the Attorney General of India (Article 76), who must be a person qualified to be appointed a judge of the Supreme Court, to advise the Union government on legal matters.

text: 49. When a resolution to impeach the President is to be moved in either House of Parliament, a written notice must be given. How many days in advance must this notice be provided?
explanation: For the impeachment of the President (Article 61), a 14 days' written notice must be given, and it must be signed by at least one-fourth of the total members of the House that framed the charges.

text: 50. Before a resolution for the impeachment of the President can be introduced in a House of Parliament, it must be signed by what fraction of the total members of that House?
explanation: The impeachment charges must be signed by at least one-fourth (1/4th) of the members of the House that initiated the charges, alongside a 14-day notice.

text: 51. To successfully pass an impeachment resolution against the President in either House of Parliament, what specific type of majority is constitutionally mandated?

options.text: A simple majority of members present and voting
A special majority of 2/3rds of members present and voting
A special majority of 2/3rds of the TOTAL membership of the House

explanation: The impeachment of the President requires the strictest majority in the Indian Constitution: a special majority of not less than two-thirds (2/3rds) of the TOTAL membership of the House.

text: 52. In the Presidential Electoral College, the value of the vote of an MLA (Member of Legislative Assembly) varies from state to state. What is the primary factor that determines this value?

options.text: The geographical area of the state
The population of the state as per the 1971 census
The GDP contribution of the state
The number of Lok Sabha seats in the state

explanation: The value of an MLA's vote is determined by dividing the total population of the state (currently based on the 1971 census) by the total number of elected members in the state legislative assembly, and then dividing the quotient by 1000.

text: 53. How is the value of the vote of an elected Member of Parliament (MP) calculated in a Presidential election?

options.text: It is exactly equal to the highest MLA vote value.
It is a fixed constitutional value of 1000.
By dividing the total value of votes of all MLAs of all states by the total number of elected MPs.
By dividing the total population of India by the total number of MPs.

explanation: To ensure parity between the States and the Union, the value of an MP's vote is calculated by taking the total value of votes of all elected MLAs of all states and dividing it by the total number of elected MPs (Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha).

text: 54. While the President is impeached by a strict 2/3rd majority of the total membership, how is the Vice President of India removed from office?

options.text: By the same impeachment process as the President (Article 61).
By an 'effective majority' in the Rajya Sabha and a simple majority in the Lok Sabha.
By the President's discretion on the advice of the Prime Minister.

explanation: Under Article 67, the Vice President can be removed by a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members of the Rajya Sabha (an effective majority) and agreed to by the Lok Sabha (simple majority). No formal impeachment is required.

text: 55. Which two individuals hold the record for being the longest-serving Vice Presidents of India, having completed two full consecutive terms?
explanation: Dr. S. Radhakrishnan (1952–1962) and Mohammad Hamid Ansari (2007–2017) are the only two Vice Presidents of India to have served two full terms in office.

text: 56. Who was the first Vice President of India to die while in office?
explanation: Krishan Kant (Vice President from 1997 to 2002) was the first Vice President of India to die in office.

text: 57. Is the pardoning power of the President under Article 72 subject to judicial review?

options.text: No, it is an absolute power immune from judicial scrutiny.
Yes, but only if the pardon involves a death sentence.
Yes, it is subject to limited judicial review if the decision is arbitrary, mala fide, or discriminatory.
No, it can only be reviewed by Parliament.

explanation: In cases like Epuru Sudhakar (2006), the Supreme Court ruled that the pardoning power of the President (and Governor) is subject to judicial review if the order was passed without application of mind, is mala fide, or suffers from arbitrariness.

text: 58. In the event of a National Emergency (Article 352), the President can proclaim it only upon receiving a written recommendation from:
explanation: Introduced by the 44th Amendment Act (1978) to prevent misuse, the President can proclaim a National Emergency only after receiving a written recommendation from the Union Cabinet (not just the Prime Minister).

text: 59. Article 87 mandates the President to deliver a 'Special Address' to both Houses of Parliament. When exactly does this address take place?

options.text: At the beginning of every single parliamentary session (Monsoon, Winter, Budget).
At the commencement of the first session after each general election and the first session of each year.
Only when the government loses a no-confidence motion.
On Republic Day and Independence Day.

explanation: Article 87 specifies that the President shall address both Houses assembled together at the commencement of the first session after each general election to the Lok Sabha and at the commencement of the first session of each year (typically the Budget session).

text: 60. Which of the following statements regarding the salary and allowances of the Vice President of India is correct?

options.text: They receive a separate salary designated exclusively for the post of Vice President.
They draw their salary entirely from their home state's consolidated fund.
The Constitution does not fix any salary for the Vice President in that capacity; they draw the regular salary of the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
They receive no salary, only government accommodations and perks.

explanation: The Constitution has not fixed any salary for the Vice President in that capacity. They draw their salary in their role as the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

text: 61. A person cannot be elected as President if they hold an 'office of profit'. However, the Constitution explicitly exempts certain offices from being considered an office of profit. Which of the following is NOT an exempted office?

options.text: The sitting President or Vice-President of the Union
A Minister of the Union or any State
The Chairman of a Public Sector Undertaking (PSU)

explanation: Under Article 58, a sitting President, Vice-President, Governor, and Ministers of the Union or States are NOT deemed to hold an office of profit and are eligible to contest. The Chairman of a PSU, however, holds a strict office of profit.

text: 62. The President has various 'Diplomatic Powers'. Which of the following statements accurately describes these powers?

options.text: The President can sign international treaties without any parliamentary approval.
International treaties and agreements are negotiated and concluded on behalf of the President, but they are subject to the approval of the Parliament.
Only the Prime Minister has the power to conclude treaties; the President has no diplomatic role.
The President must personally travel to sign all international treaties.

explanation: International treaties and agreements are negotiated and concluded on behalf of the President. However, they are always subject to the approval of the Parliament.

text: 63. The President's 'Military Powers' include the supreme command of the defence forces. In this capacity, the President can declare war or conclude peace. This power is subject to the approval of:
explanation: While the President is the Supreme Commander of the armed forces (Article 53) and can declare war or conclude peace, the exercise of this power is strictly regulated by law and subject to the approval of the Parliament.

text: 64. How long does the President have to exercise a 'Pocket Veto' (taking no action on a bill passed by Parliament)?

options.text: There is no time limit; the period is indefinite.

explanation: The Indian Constitution does not prescribe any time limit within which the President has to declare their assent or refusal. This allows the President to exercise a 'pocket veto' by keeping the bill pending for an indefinite period (unlike the US President, who has 10 days).

text: 65. When a State Legislature passes a bill, the Governor can reserve it for the consideration of the President under Article 200. What is the President's power regarding such a reserved state bill?

options.text: The President must give their assent within 6 months.
The President can only use a pocket veto, not an absolute veto.
The President can return an ordinary bill for reconsideration, but if the state legislature passes it again, the President is STILL not bound to give their assent.
The President cannot withhold assent if the state passes it a second time.

explanation: Unlike parliamentary bills (where the President must give assent if the bill is passed a second time), for state bills reserved by the Governor, the President is NOT constitutionally bound to give their assent even if the state legislature passes the bill a second time.

text: 66. During a Financial Emergency (Article 360), which of the following directives can the President issue?

options.text: Suspension of the right to move courts for Fundamental Rights enforcement.
Reduction of salaries and allowances of all or any class of persons serving the Union, including Supreme Court and High Court judges.
Dissolution of all State Legislative Assemblies immediately.
Transfer of all private bank funds to the Consolidated Fund of India.

explanation: Under Article 360 (Financial Emergency), the President can issue directions for the reduction of salaries and allowances of any class of persons serving the Union or a State, including the Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts.

text: 67. If a candidate in a Presidential election secures 1/6th of the valid votes polled, what happens to their security deposit of ₹15,000?

options.text: It is forfeited and transferred to the Consolidated Fund of India.
It is refunded to the candidate.
It is distributed among the winning candidate's campaign funds.
It is donated to the Prime Minister's Relief Fund.

explanation: The security deposit of ₹15,000 in the Reserve Bank of India is refunded to the candidate if they successfully secure at least one-sixth (1/6th) of the valid votes polled. If they fail to secure 1/6th, the deposit is forfeited.

text: 68. Which constitutional amendment explicitly made it mandatory for the President to give their assent to Constitutional Amendment Bills?
explanation: The 24th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1971 amended Article 368 to provide that when a Constitutional Amendment Bill is presented to the President, 'he shall give his assent', eliminating any veto power over such bills.

text: 69. What is the precise constitutional terminology used to describe the removal of the President versus the Vice President?

options.text: The President is 'Removed'; the Vice President is 'Impeached'.
The President is 'Impeached' (Article 61); the Vice President is 'Removed' via a resolution (Article 67).
Both undergo a 'Vote of No Confidence'.

explanation: The Constitution strictly uses the term 'Impeachment' only for the President (Article 61). For the Vice President, Supreme Court Judges, and the CAG, it uses the term 'Removal'.

text: 70. Who has the authority to appoint the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners under Article 324?
explanation: The President of India appoints key constitutional functionaries, including the Chief Election Commissioner, the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG), the Chairman of the UPSC, and the Governors of states.

text: 71. Certain types of bills require the prior recommendation or sanction of the President before they can be introduced in Parliament. Which of the following bills falls into this category?

options.text: A bill to amend the Fundamental Rights
A bill for the formation of new States or alteration of boundaries
An Ordinary Bill originating in the Rajya Sabha
A bill to abolish a State Legislative Council

explanation: Under Article 3 of the Constitution, a bill for the formation of new states or alteration of boundaries/names of existing states can be introduced in Parliament ONLY on the prior recommendation of the President.

text: 72. When the Vice President of India acts as the President due to a vacancy, who performs the duties of the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha?

options.text: The Vice President performs both roles simultaneously
The senior-most member of the Rajya Sabha
The Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
A new Chairman temporarily appointed by the President

explanation: When the Vice President acts as the President, they cease to perform the duties of the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. During this period, those duties are performed by the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

text: 73. Under Article 62 of the Constitution, an election to fill a vacancy caused by the expiration of the regular term of office of the President shall be completed:

options.text: Within six months after the expiration of the term
Before the expiration of the term
Within three months after the expiration of the term
Whenever the Election Commission deems it appropriate

explanation: Article 62 mandates that an election to fill a vacancy caused by the expiration of the term of office of President shall be completed BEFORE the expiration of the term.

text: 74. If the office of the President falls vacant due to resignation, removal, or death, a new President is elected within six months. What is the duration of the newly elected President's term?

options.text: The remainder of the predecessor's term
A full term of 5 years from the date they assume office
Six months, after which another election is held
Until the next general elections for the Lok Sabha

explanation: Unlike the US system where the Vice President completes the remainder of the term, a newly elected President in India serves a full term of five years from the date they enter upon their office.

text: 75. Which of the following is true regarding the comparison of the Ordinance-making power of the President (Article 123) and the Governor (Article 213)?

options.text: Both can issue ordinances on any subject in the Union List.
The Governor cannot make an ordinance without the President's instructions on certain bills (e.g., those requiring President's prior sanction).
The President's ordinance has a maximum lifespan of 1 year, while the Governor's is 6 months.
The Governor cannot withdraw their ordinance at any time, unlike the President.

explanation: The Governor’s ordinance-making power is subject to certain restrictions. The Governor cannot make an ordinance without the instructions from the President if a bill containing the same provisions would have required the previous sanction of the President for its introduction.

text: 76. To prevent non-serious candidates from contesting, the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act specifies minimum proposer requirements. What is the requirement for a Presidential candidate?

options.text: 20 electors as proposers and 20 as seconders
50 electors as proposers and 50 as seconders
100 electors as proposers and 50 as seconders
10 electors as proposers and 10 as seconders

explanation: A candidate for the President's office needs at least 50 electors as proposers and 50 electors as seconders. (For the Vice President, the requirement is 20 proposers and 20 seconders).

text: 77. If the electoral college for the President or Vice President is incomplete (for example, if a State Legislative Assembly has been dissolved), what happens to the election?

options.text: The election is postponed until the Assembly is reconstituted.
The election proceeds, and it cannot be challenged on the ground that the electoral college was incomplete.
The President appoints an acting official until elections can be held.
The Supreme Court must grant special permission to hold the election.

explanation: According to the 11th Constitutional Amendment Act (1961), the election of a President or Vice President cannot be challenged on the ground of any vacancy in the appropriate electoral college.

text: 78. Which Article explicitly states that the executive power of the Union shall be vested in the President and shall be exercised by him either directly or through officers subordinate to him?
explanation: Article 53 of the Constitution vests the executive power of the Union in the President and commands that it be exercised in accordance with the Constitution.

text: 79. If the Supreme Court declares the election of a person as President or Vice President void, what happens to the acts done by them in the execution of their office prior to that declaration?

options.text: All their acts are immediately considered null and void.
The acts are reviewed by the Parliament for validation.
The acts remain valid and are not invalidated by the court's declaration.
Only financial decisions remain valid; legislative assents are revoked.

explanation: Under Article 71(2), if the election of a person as President or Vice-President is declared void by the Supreme Court, acts done by him in the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of the office on or before the date of the decision of the Supreme Court shall NOT be invalidated.

text: 80. The President of India can be removed from office by a process of impeachment for 'violation of the Constitution'. In which house of Parliament can these impeachment charges be initiated?

options.text: Only in a joint sitting of both Houses

explanation: According to Article 61, the impeachment charges against the President can be initiated in either House of Parliament, requiring a 14-day notice and the signatures of 1/4th of the members of that House.

text: 81. According to Article 74, the Council of Ministers aids and advises the President. Can the President return this advice for reconsideration?

options.text: No, the advice is strictly binding in the first instance.
Yes, he can require the Council to reconsider the advice once, but is bound by the reconsidered advice.
Yes, he can return it an unlimited number of times.
Only if the Supreme Court approves the reconsideration.

explanation: The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act (1978) added a provision allowing the President to require the Council of Ministers to reconsider such advice. However, the President is bound to act in accordance with the advice tendered after such reconsideration.

text: 82. Who among the following is constitutionally empowered to declare any area as a 'Scheduled Area' and alter its boundaries?

options.text: The Governor of the respective State

explanation: Under the Fifth Schedule, the President is empowered to declare an area to be a Scheduled Area. He can also increase or decrease its area, alter its boundary lines, or revoke such designation in consultation with the Governor of the state.

text: 83. Political scientists classify veto powers into four types. Which of the following veto powers is NOT possessed by the President of India?
explanation: The President of India has Absolute, Suspensive, and Pocket vetoes. The 'Qualified Veto' (which can be overridden by the legislature with a higher majority) is possessed by the American President, not the Indian President.

text: 84. Under Article 143, the President has the power to consult the Supreme Court. If the President refers a question of law or public importance to the Supreme Court, is the Court's opinion binding on the President?

options.text: No, the opinion is advisory and not binding on the President.
It is binding only if it relates to a pre-constitution treaty.
It is binding only if it is delivered by a 5-judge Constitutional Bench.

explanation: The Supreme Court's opinion under its Advisory Jurisdiction (Article 143) is only advisory in nature. The President is not bound to follow the opinion given by the Supreme Court.

text: 85. Article 78 of the Constitution defines the duties of the Prime Minister in respect to furnishing information to the President. Which of the following is NOT one of these duties?

options.text: To communicate all decisions of the Council of Ministers to the President.
To submit proposals for legislation to the President.
To seek the President's prior approval for all Cabinet-level portfolio assignments.
To submit for the consideration of the Council of Ministers any matter on which a decision has been taken by a Minister but not considered by the Council, if the President requires it.

explanation: Article 78 outlines the PM's duty to communicate decisions and legislative proposals to the President. It does NOT require the PM to seek the President's prior approval for assigning portfolios to Cabinet ministers; the PM advises the President on who to appoint, but portfolio allocation is the PM's prerogative.
